newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF mulls expanding standby loan to Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: IMF mulls expanding standby loan to Pakistan.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday it would consider extending its $600 million standby loan to Pakistan and making additional funds available.

"Following recent IMF staff talks with the Pakistani authorities, the IMF's Executive Board is expected to consider an extension of the current standby credit, as well as an increase in the total amount available thereunder," a statement from the IMF resident representative in Islamabad said.
The statement said the IMF board was expected to meet in the second week of December for this purpose.

Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic adviser to Pakistan's caretaker prime minister, told a news conference earlier that he expected the IMF to increase the amount of the standby loan beyond the $320 million still undisbursed.
"We expect to get more than $320 million which the previous (Benazir Bhutto-led) government was to get," Burki said, but did not say how large an expansion of the loan was envisaged.
He said the conditions of the loan had not changed from those agreed on October 22 by the Bhutto government, which was dismissed by President Farooq Leghari on November 5.

The ousted government had announced a sweeping package of spending cuts and higher taxes, along with a 7.86 percent devalution of the rupee against the dollar, to persuade the IMF to resume standby payments and avert a foreign exchange crisis.
Burki said Pakistan's foreign reserves had risen to $700 million from $587 million on November 5. "When we took over the country was on the verge of economic collapse," he declared.
"We were standing on the abyss," Burki said. "We would have been reduced from a credit economy to a cash economy had the president not dismissed the previous government."

He said the Bhutto administration had collapsed partly because of economic problems that included depletion of foreign reserves, collapse of state-run banks, uncontrolled government spending, recession in the textile industry, rampant corruption and erosion in real income due to inflation and unemployment.
Burki, who will travel to Washington on Sunday, said the standby loan, originally programmed to finish in March 1997, was now likely to be rephased over nine or 10 months.
He said he would urge the IMF to convert the loan, which began a year ago but stalled after two tranches were paid, into an enhanced structural adjustment facility. He gave no details.
